transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-01 14:30 PST — duration ~62m — attendees: Maya, Ethan (Redwood) / Liam, Priya, Carlos, Nina (Aurora)

Summary: quick technical deep dive on Redwood KV cache evictions and paging under Aurora's long-context streaming workload. Discussed prefix reuse thrash, eviction policies (LRU vs segmented), paging to host memory, sticky routing, and proposed mitigations (pinning, dedicated pools, prefetching). Agreed next steps to run targeted benchmarks and share logs.

Topics: KV cache eviction, paging/offload, long-context streaming, prefix reuse/TTL, batching effects on KV hit rate, quantization impact on memory, VPC/private deployment considerations for pinned cache pools.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for taking the deep dive, um this is Maya from Redwood, we got Ethan on the call as well for the SE side. can you all hear me okay?
[00:04] Liam Chen: yeah can hear you, thanks for doing this, we've been hitting these weird evictions in prod and it's spiking P99 latency.
[00:10] Ethan Ross: cool, yeah we've been reading the traces you sent, looks like repeated cache churn when you hit long multi-turn streams, and there's some prefix reuse across sessions. interesting pattern.
[00:18] Priya Singh: right, so quick context: our agents send ~30–90k token sessions, lots of shared intro prompts between users, and sometimes we do multi-agent routing where prefixes are reused across tasks. evictions start around the 45–60 minute mark.
[00:30] Carlos Rivera: and to add, memory pressure on the inference nodes climbs slowly then spikes and the pods OOM or get throttled, then requests fallback to a smaller model which kills our quality.
[00:40] Ethan Ross: okay so two things likely: 1) long-context increases KV size per session, and 2) prefix reuse across concurrent sessions is causing thrash — keys are inserted and evicted repeatedly. Our default eviction is an LRU with soft limits but when pressure hits it can cause segments to get cleared.
[00:55] Priya Singh: is that LRU global per-process or per-client? we've seen cases where one noisy client evicts others.
[01:02] Ethan Ross: good question — by default it's per-process global LRU for the serving worker. we do support segmented caches (per-customer or per-model pools) but they're opt-in and require config changes, also some private deployments pin prefixes.
[01:12] Liam Chen: hmm segmented sounds promising. what about paging to host RAM or disk? we saw references to 'paging' in the docs but unclear on latency impact.
[01:20] Ethan Ross: paging is hybrid — we can spill colder KV entries to host memory (NUMA-aware) and read them back, but that's much slower than a full GPU-resident hit. disk-backed paging exists for Dedicated/Private but it's a last resort and adds tens to hundreds of ms per miss, so not great for P95.
[01:34] Maya Patel: and note, for hosted we prefer keeping hot KV on GPU as much as possible, but with very long contexts you hit the capacity wall unless you shard or pin.
[01:42] Nina Alvarez: what exactly do you mean by pin? can we pin the system prompt so it never gets evicted?
[01:46] Ethan Ross: yes, pinning marks a keyset as non-evictable up to a configured memory fraction. common pattern: pin shared intro prefixes or system prompts so reuse doesn't cause churn. downside: pinned keys reduce available GPU memory for new tokens.
[01:57] Priya Singh: if we pin the intro prompts for ~2000 concurrent users, memory might go up a lot. any heuristics?
[02:04] Ethan Ross: heuristics: measure distinct prefix cardinality and frequency. if top 10% prefixes cover 70% of requests, pinning top 10% often pays off. otherwise segmented pools per-customer with reserved capacity works better.
[02:16] Carlos Rivera: segmentation seems admin-heavy, plus we run in our VPC with private deployment. would Redwood manage segmentation or we configure?
[02:23] Maya Patel: for Private deployments, we provide the config and assist with rollout; we can also enable per-tenant pools and autoscale policies so noisy tenants don't evict others.
[02:31] Liam Chen: ok that sounds useful. what's the impact of batching on KV hit rates? we want high throughput so we batch aggressively.
[02:38] Ethan Ross: batching groups requests and can increase reuse because KV is shared across the batch if the sequence prefixes align. but large batch windows also increase transient KV pressure because multiple sessions are advancing caches at similar times. we tune batch size to trade throughput vs per-session memory growth. continuous batching with prefix-aware grouping helps.
[02:53] Priya Singh: prefix-aware grouping? explain a bit.
[02:55] Ethan Ross: we group requests by recent prefix fingerprint so requests that will benefit from the same KV entries are batched together; that reduces cache misses inside the batch and reduces write amplification. it's an advanced option on the runtime.
[03:06] Nina Alvarez: earlier you said quantization affects memory. we use int8 quantized models — does that change KV size?
[03:11] Ethan Ross: quantization affects model weights and KV storage format slightly; int8 can shrink KV footprint by ~10–20% depending on implementation, but it also changes kernel selection and can impact throughput. it's not a silver bullet for extreme long-context; you still need sharding/paging/pinning.
[03:24] Liam Chen: ok. we also noticed eviction spikes correlated with rolling deploys of newer model versions. any recommendations?
[03:30] Ethan Ross: during rollout we reinitialize caches on worker replacement; that leads to cold caches and a temporary surge in KB traffic and memory rebuilds. strategy: do canary routing with warmed caches, or use pre-warming where you seed new workers with hot prefixes. we also support graceful cache migration in Dedicated/Private if you keep kernel compatibility.
[03:45] Priya Singh: what's the warm-up cost for a 90k token session?
[03:48] Ethan Ross: depends, but building the KV for long context is O(tokens) and initial population will generate storage pressure. for 90k tokens the first few minutes will be heavy; we try to stream and reuse earlier prefixes and use prefix compaction to summarize older context to a compressed representation.
[04:02] Carlos Rivera: prefix compaction — can you expand, is that lossy?
[04:05] Ethan Ross: it's a summarization step: for very old context we can replace detailed token-level KV with a condensed summary embedding or compressed state. that trades off perfect rollback for much smaller memory use. works for many chat use-cases but not when exact token-level context is mandatory.
[04:19] Maya Patel: I want to step through Aurora's failure trace we saw — Ethan, can you call out the key patterns?
[04:25] Ethan Ross: yes — in the trace we see: repeated insert/delete of near-identical keys, high churn on nodes 3 and 4, and a spike in GC/allocator stalls right before OOM. the pattern suggests a hot set larger than GPU KV capacity, and eviction thrash because prefixes are highly overlapping across sessions.
[04:40] Priya Singh: overlapping how — same system prompt + small user-specific tokens?
[04:44] Ethan Ross: exactly — everyone starts with the same 500-token system prompt, then small divergent branches. so the large shared prefix is being duplicated in cache for each session because we keep per-session KV namespaces currently. that duplicative storage leads to memory blowout.
[04:57] Liam Chen: so can we dedupe those shared prefixes across sessions?
[05:00] Ethan Ross: yes — dedupe shared prefixes at insertion time by canonicalizing prefix keys and using shared references; that reduces duplication drastically. downside: introduces cross-session coupling for cache lifecycle which changes eviction semantics and requires careful TTL.
[05:12] Carlos Rivera: are there any security/regulatory concerns if we share prefix references across tenants? we run multiple product lines in same infra.
[05:20] Maya Patel: good catch — for multi-tenant you must avoid cross-tenant dedupe. Redwood supports namespace isolation and dedupe can be enabled safely within tenant namespaces. for multi-tenant pools you should use per-tenant pools or tag keys with tenant ids.
[05:33] Priya Singh: for our private deployment in VPC, can we get a dedicated pool per product team?
[05:37] Ethan Ross: yes, that's a supported option and recommended for noisy neighbors. we can set reserved memory per pool and autoscale rules so a spike in one pool doesn't affect others.
[05:46] Nina Alvarez: back to paging — you said disk paging adds big latencies. any middle ground like host memory SSD-backed swap?
[05:53] Ethan Ross: host RAM spill is the first line; if host RAM exhausted we can spill to NVMe. NVMe spill adds ~20–80ms depending on IO, which for some throughput-oriented use-cases is tolerable. we generally only recommend NVMe spill for Dedicated/Private where customers accept the latency tradeoff.
[06:08] Liam Chen: what about fallback strategies — if you detect eviction thrash do you route to smaller model automatically?
[06:14] Ethan Ross: yes we have routing policies: fallback to lighter model, route to dedicated capacity, or reject requests. automated fallback is configurable and we can set SLO-based thresholds for actions.
[06:23] Priya Singh: are there telemetry signals we should watch? we saw only memory RSS and OOMs in CloudWatch; what else?
[06:29] Ethan Ross: important signals: KV insert/delete rate, KV hit ratio, per-prefix cardinality, allocator stalls, paging I/O rates, and batch size histograms. Redwood Console shows token-level cost and per-model cache metrics; we'll share a dashboard template.
[06:44] Maya Patel: ok can we go over a proposed mitigation path for Aurora? quick bullet list.
[06:47] Ethan Ross: sure — 1) isolate hot prefixes: enable per-tenant pools, 2) dedupe shared system prefixes, 3) pin top-N frequent prefixes (if cardinality low), 4) enable host-RAM spill with NVMe fallback for non-latency-critical routes, 5) tune batching with prefix-aware grouping, 6) add cache pre-warming during rolling deploys, 7) instrument KV hit ratio and top prefix cardinality dashboards.
[07:09] Liam Chen: realistic timeline to test this? we can spin staging with same workload.
[07:13] Ethan Ross: we can run a staged test in 48–72 hours once we get sanitized workload and logs. blueprint: run 24h stress with 1k concurrent sessions to reproduce thrash, then iterate configs.
[07:22] Priya Singh: ok i'll get the dataset and traces to you by Thursday, that's 2026-12-03.
[07:26] Maya Patel: we'll prioritize reproducer and bench; Ethan will own logs analysis.
[07:29] Carlos Rivera: question — any quick config change we can try today to reduce spike risk?
[07:33] Ethan Ross: two low-risk changes: reduce per-worker KV capacity soft-limit slightly to force earlier segmentation, and enable prefix compaction for context older than N tokens. both are reversible and low-risk.
[07:44] Liam Chen: great, we'll try those on staging.
[07:47] Nina Alvarez: two housekeeping Qs: will enabling dedupe require code changes? and does it affect auditing?
[07:52] Ethan Ross: dedupe is runtime config for Private/Dedicated (no code change), and auditing is unaffected because keys are namespaced — we can still log access per-tenant. we'll include audit log examples in the docs.
[08:03] Maya Patel: all right, let's recap next steps and owners. Ethan: logs collection and initial config patch and benchmark plan. Priya: workload and traces by 2026-12-03. Maya: send KV tuning guide and dashboards by 2026-12-02. schedule follow-up week of 2026-12-07.
[08:18] Liam Chen: thanks much for doing this, felt productive.
[08:21] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
